Oecb4a.text:
Find rail and road safety guidance, performance information, consultations and publications.
Welcome to the September edition of ORR’s stakeholder newsletter.
A pressing focus for us as a regulator is ensuring a safer railway for passengers, workers and the general public. We were therefore deeply concerned by August’s derailments at Lewes and Wickford. Our thoughts are with those affected and we are investigating the circumstances of the incidents.
Such incidents are thankfully rare, but maintaining that record depends on continual vigilance, learning, and improvement. ORR's role is to ensure that investigations are thorough, that the industry's response is evidence-based, and that any lessons needed to manage future risks are identified and acted upon.
Alongside our investigative and regulatory work, ORR's legal team plays a vital role in protecting the public and supporting a railway and road network that works for everyone. Their expertise helps ensure that safety obligations are properly understood and enforced, that operators and infrastructure managers are held to account where necessary, and that regulatory decisions are fair, robust and capable of withstanding scrutiny.
Whether supporting prosecutions, advising on complex regulatory issues, or helping to shape the framework within which industry operates, our work is fundamental to achieving better outcomes for passengers, road users and freight customers.
That contribution was evident again in August when Network Rail was fined £1.2million after it pleaded guilty to an offence under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 following the collapse of a wall in September 2022 near Rugby station.
The boundary wall beside a car park at the station collapsed onto 81-year-old pedestrian Edward Hanlon, as he walked along the adjacent path. Although Network Rail owned the wall and remained responsible for its repair and maintenance, undocumented redevelopment of the station car park by a previous tenant led to the mistaken assumption that responsibility lay elsewhere.
ORR's investigation found that the wall had therefore been omitted from Network Rail's inspection regime. The organisation had failed to identify both the discrepancy in its boundary records or the wall's deteriorating condition. These failings meant the risk the wall posed to members of the public went unidentified. Mr Hanlon passed away in January 2025 from lymphoma. A statement from his daughter indicated he never fully recovered from his injuries.
We will continue to use the full range of our regulatory and legal powers where it is in the public interest to do so.
Through this work, and through our broader regulatory activities, we remain committed to protecting people while enabling safe, reliable and efficient rail and road systems that serve everyone.
We have pre-approved a new framework track access agreement between HS1 Limited (London St. Pancras Highspeed) and Virgin Trains, supporting economic growth and international travel.
Virgin Trains will be able to operate up to 20 daily return international services between London and Paris, and Brussels and Amsterdam from 1 October 2030 through to 31 December 2040.

Our detailed investigation and decision to prosecute followed Network Rail’s failure to inspect or maintain the wall after undocumented redevelopment work by a previous tenant led to a mistaken assumption over the station boundary. These failings led to the wall’s deteriorating condition going unidentified and the consequences that followed.

Oaeb9c.title: Volunteering delivers purpose - but also anxiety
Oaeb9c.text:
New research has found that people who volunteer have a greater purpose in life, but it comes at a cost, with volunteering also linked to higher levels of anxiety.
The study was led by psychologists from the Research Centre for Better Living at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) and involved data from 7,146 adults in England who participated in the Taking Part Survey, carried out by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.
Volunteering is regarded as a net benefit to society, often focusing on the unmet needs of individuals and communities, and the economic contribution of volunteers is substantial, with the UN estimating it accounts for around 2.5% of global GDP.
Published in the journal Behavioral Sciences , the new research found that any form of volunteering in the previous 12 months was associated with participants reporting a stronger sense that their lives were worthwhile.
After controlling for variables linked to subjective wellbeing and loneliness outcomes – gender, age, level of deprivation, health and employment status – the effect of volunteering on people reporting that their life was worthwhile was more than 1.5 times greater than the effect of being in employment.
The researchers believe this could be because unlike employment, volunteering usually involves activities that are chosen because they are personally meaningful. It is often in charitable or not-for-profit sectors, and being able to help a particular cause may strengthen feelings of purpose.
However, the study also found that volunteering was not linked to greater happiness, higher life satisfaction or lower levels of loneliness, despite volunteering often suggested as a form of ‘social prescribing’. And crucially, it found that volunteering predicted significantly higher levels of anxiety.
The findings that volunteering is associated with a greater sense of meaning (eudaimonic wellbeing) but not positive feelings such as happiness (hedonic wellbeing) could be because meaningful activities come with emotional costs as well as benefits.
The researchers suggest people might gain a stronger sense of purpose through volunteering precisely because it involves commitment and effort, sometimes in sectors that involve emotionally distressing situations, which may explain the relationship with anxiety.
"Volunteering is often promoted as something that boosts wellbeing, and our findings partly support that idea. However, the picture is more complex.
“We found evidence that volunteering was linked to greater purpose, but not to greater happiness. In fact, volunteers reported slightly higher anxiety. That doesn't mean volunteering is harmful, but it does suggest that meaningful activities may come with emotional costs as well as benefits.
"Volunteers provide enormous benefits to society, and our findings should not be interpreted as a reason to volunteer less. Instead, they highlight the importance of supporting volunteers properly and recognising that people who give their time to help others may also need support themselves.
"As a society, we often focus on whether an activity makes people happy. Our findings suggest that volunteering may offer something different: a sense that life matters and has purpose. That may be one of the most important contributions volunteering makes, even if it is not always accompanied by greater happiness.
"Perhaps our most unexpected finding was that volunteering was a stronger predictor of a sense that life is worthwhile than being in employment. Employment provides income, structure and social connection, but volunteering may offer something different: an opportunity to choose work that reflects personal values and directly helps others.”

Of9422.title: Five ways to enjoy fashion without overconsuming
Of9422.text:
By Cathrine Jansson-Boyd , Anglia Ruskin University
Fashion lovers are generally associated with bursting wardrobes and chasing the latest trends. But that reputation is beginning to shift.
In the last few years, market surveys have found that around a third of shoppers are now buying second hand clothing . For gen Z, this figure increases to just under half. Giant hauls from fast fashion brands were once the trend – but an eye for vintage bargains and pre-worn fits is now more on point.
Though buying used is far preferential to buying new, overconsumption can still be a problem with second-hand clothing. That’s because buying used often supplements, rather than replaces, fast fashion habits.
If you love fashion, but want to indulge in your hobby without falling into the trap of overconsumption, here are five tips.
“Shopping your closet” – creating new looks with the existing pieces in your wardrobe – has been trending online for a while. Putting some thought into how you can restyle existing pieces will help you to shift your focus from buying something, to becoming creative.
Research has shown that a small and versatile wardrobe that can easily be mixed and matched into several outfits fosters creativity as your brain must solve styling puzzles with limited items. It also generates feelings of satisfaction and enjoyment. This is important as being content with your clothing choices is linked to general wellbeing.
It can be helpful to schedule a dedicated wardrobe date and treat styling your closet like a fun puzzle rather than a chore. Creativity tends to flow better when under less pressure, so don’t try to build your creative cognitive styling muscles when you are in a rush.
To get inspiration flowing, try searching sites like Pinterest. Type in exact terms like “oversized blazer outfit” to discover fresh styling ideas for pieces sitting in your closet. Set yourself a challenge for 10 days not to wear any combination you have worn before.
And just so you don’t forget: snap quick mirror photos of any outfit combinations that work well so you have a personal outfit catalogue ready for busy mornings.
Having too many clothes can lead to choice overload , when the difficulty of decision exceeds our cognitive ability to make a choice.
Generally, people tend to find it easier to make a choice when they have less to choose from. If you have two T-shirts, your brain can decide in seconds. But if you have 18 T-shirts, wardrobe paralysis kicks in.
Treat sorting through your clothes as an interactive styling project. Reorganising by colour or silhouette can help you to rediscover forgotten favourites and appreciate the craftsmanship of items you already own, as well as making it easier to choose.
Try buying clothing as a collector or curator. This means that you should select unique, high-quality pieces based on your personal preference and their long-term value. Look past trends by evaluating fabric weight, seam stitching, lining quality and natural fibres (like wool, linen, or silk) before buying, ensuring each addition to your wardrobe is built to last.
Keep a running list of missing baseline pieces or specific archive designs. Planning ahead limits the likelihood of making an impulse purchase, which may lead to regret . Taking 48 hours to think it over also reduces the chances of making the wrong decision.
Craft a clear vision of your personal aesthetic focusing on your favoured silhouettes, colour palettes and textures, so that every prospective purchase must earn its place alongside your existing collection.
Building a wardrobe based on your specific personal taste allows you to treat your personal style as a fine art rather than a fast-fashion race. You’ll also probably keep your garments for longer as items people care for tend to become tangible extensions of their identity .

Oc76a3.title: Most dog attacks are preventable – new research
Oc76a3.text:
A new analysis focusing on dog attacks on humans in the UK suggests that most incidents are preventable and committed by a wide variety of breeds rather than solely by highly publicised ‘dangerous dogs’ – and owners have a key part to play in prevention.
The new report, entitled Safety Around Dogs: A Process Analysis of Dog Bites , was commissioned by Battersea Dogs and Cats Home and carried out by Anglia Ruskin University (ARU), and examined court records, hospital admission, policy and survey data.
The report analysed 130 dog bite incidents from court data between 2020 and 2025 and found that the circumstances behind dog attacks are highly variable. Of the court data, owner failure to control a dog was the single most common cause, blamed for 32% of cases. The report describe these as unprovoked attacks where a dog jumps up and bites a passer-by in a public place.
A total of 24 cases were a result of the dog escaping either from a property or being tethered and then biting, suggesting that the dog was not appropriately secured by its owner.
All data sets analysed within the report showed that dog attacks involve a wide variety of breeds and that bites are not confined to dogs covered by breed-specific legislation.
Researchers also found that adults account for the majority of victims in both court cases and hospital admission data, despite public concern often focusing on attacks involving children. A notable 14% of people who completed the survey had been bitten three or more times.
As a result of the findings, the report urges both dog owners and policymakers to use similar situational crime prevention measures that are deployed in most other antisocial behaviour scenarios to reduce the risk of attack.
Recommendations set out in the report include better education about safe interactions with dogs, keeping dogs on a lead in higher-risk public settings, and better “dog-proofing” of homes to protect visitors, postal workers and delivery drivers.
The researchers also call for consideration of measures such as enhanced dog registration, stronger links between registration and microchipping, and a mandatory code of practice for dog owners.

Od45e7.title: Denise enjoys much calmer second graduation day
Od45e7.text:
Denise Erica Da Costa Silva at her graduation ceremony at Peterborough Cathedral this week after completing a Master's Degree in International Business Management at ARU Peterborough
A mother-of-four who fled domestic abuse in her home country to build a new life in the UK is celebrating her second graduation from ARU Peterborough – which was considerably less eventful than the first.
After completing her undergraduate studies with ARU Peterborough in 2025, Denise Erica Da Costa Silva went straight from Peterborough Cathedral to hospital to give birth to her fourth child.
Last September, she began her postgraduate course in International Business Management , and she celebrated her second ARU Peterborough graduation at Peterborough Cathedral this week.
Denise had moved to the UK in 2019 with her oldest three children after making the difficult decision to leave an abusive relationship and start again. Determined to create a safer and more secure future for her family, she arrived in Peterborough ready to rebuild her life from scratch.
Denise had previously studied Portuguese and Communication at university and built a career in banking, customer services and marketing in Angola. As she qualifies as a Portuguese citizen through her mother, she was able to settle in the UK but found that the qualifications she had gained earlier in her life were not fully recognised here.
“When I moved here it was very challenging to find work. My first job was as a part-time cleaner which made it very challenging to juggle work and childcare.”
She decided to gain UK qualifications, starting with Level 3 studies and then a Foundation course in London, but the opening of ARU Peterborough offered a life-changing possibility to gain qualifications closer to home. Being able to study locally enabled Denise to balance family responsibilities with her academic ambitions.
She successfully applied to study for an undergraduate degree in Business and Management, graduating in 2025, and has now graduated from her postgraduate studies while preparing a future PhD proposal exploring challenges within human resource management.
Denise was heavily pregnant on the day of her undergraduate graduation, but made it through the ceremony before heading straight to hospital, where she gave birth to baby Zlatan a few days later.
“I came for the ceremony and I started feeling the pain but to be honest I was so focused. I rushed from the Cathedral to the hospital straight afterwards.
“I was in considerable pain, but there was no way I was going to miss that milestone!”
Denise began her postgraduate course when Zlatan was just two months old. She added: “It was a very hard time. It was just me and the kids but because I had a lot of support from ARU Peterborough, the lecturers and my personal tutor, they gave me a lot of strength and in the end I made it.”
Denise is now pursuing a PhD qualification and hopes her story will encourage others facing adversity to pursue their ambitions. Her eldest daughter Lourdes is considering following in her footsteps by studying Business Management at ARU Peterborough next September.
“When I first started studying in the UK, I could never have imagined reaching this point. Balancing motherhood, employment and studying has not always been easy.
“My advice to others is don't allow barriers to stop you from pursuing your ambitions. Whether it is language, family commitments or a lack of confidence, there are tools and support available to help you overcome those hurdles.”

O2cb19.title: ARU is using creativity to drive economic growth
O2cb19.text:
Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) is a key partner in a new £6.75 million initiative that aims to harness the power of creative industries to accelerate economic growth in the East of England.
The programme, called CreateSci, will connect the region’s creative businesses with major tech partners including BT, ElevenLabs and industrial software company AVEVA – providing access to new technology, expertise and potential markets.
More than 250 creative businesses will benefit from the new programme, led by the University of East Anglia (UEA), helping create up to 500 skilled jobs across the region.
CreateSci is being funded by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) and delivered by the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC). It is one of only a handful of creative clusters being funded across the UK , and the first of its kind in the East of England.
The programme will be led by UEA alongside ARU, Norwich University of the Arts and the University of Suffolk, with the University of Cambridge as a project partner.
At the heart of the programme is the development of the Creative Clinic, where creative businesses and arts and humanities researchers work alongside scientists, the NHS and major employers to tackle real world challenges in relating to health, wellbeing and the environment.
It will showcase how creativity, storytelling, design and community engagement are vital to ensure scientific breakthroughs are understood, trusted and used. Using creative expertise to drive innovation, the programme will help businesses access research, build new skills, and turn ideas into products, while forging new connections with investors and partners.
CreateSci is also expected to attract further public and private investment into the region, creating new opportunities across towns, cities, rural areas and coastal communities – strengthening the East of England’s reputation as a place where creativity drives growth.
“The creative industries are one of the UK’s greatest economic strengths, and vital to the Government’s Industrial Strategy ambitions for national growth, but that growth depends on having the right skills, talent and opportunities in place in all regions.
The East of England has a strong and growing creative sector but has historically attracted less investment than many other regions.
“This cluster is unique because growth goes way beyond creative industries – into the East’s other key sectors of clean energy and life science.
“CreateSci will help businesses across the East of England develop the expertise needed in a rapidly changing sector, supporting them to innovate, grow and attract investment.
<p“We are delighted to be working alongside Norwich University of the Arts, Anglia Ruskin University, the University of Suffolk, Cambridge, industry partners and the Arts and Humanities Research Council on this shared ambition.
“Together, we are investing in the people, skills and ideas that underpin the Government’s Modern Industrial Strategy and strengthen the region’s long-term economic future.”
“Across Cambridge and the wider East of England, we have world-class scientific and technological research alongside creative businesses and communities. CreateSci provides a platform to connect this knowledge.
“At ARU, through DesignLab, one of the specialist labs within the Centre for Media, Arts and Creative Technologies (MACT) , we are particularly interested in how design-led approaches can connect research with real-world challenges, ensuring that innovation is grounded in the needs, knowledge and experiences of communities.
“Our ambition is to help build a more connected, collaborative, and resilient regional economy, generating lasting value and benefits that extend well beyond the lifetime of the programme.”

O92f8c.title: Can NAD+ supplements help us age more healthily?
O92f8c.text:
By Justin Roberts , Anglia Ruskin University
Anti-ageing supplements are everywhere, from advertising campaigns to social media feeds. Promising everything from increased energy to a longer life, they come in many forms, from powders containing multiple ingredients to single-nutrient capsules.
One molecule in particular, NAD+ , has attracted growing interest, with claims it can boost energy, improve vitality, slow ageing and even help us live longer.
But does the science support these claims? And can NAD+ supplements really help us age more healthily?
NAD+ (short for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is found in every cell in our bodies. It plays an essential role in helping our cells turn food into energy . Without it, many of the processes that keep us alive would be unable to function.
NAD+ also supports numerous enzymes and proteins, including sirtuins, which help regulate inflammation, DNA repair and the function of mitochondria , the structures responsible for producing much of the energy our cells need.
Research suggests that NAD+ levels decline as we get older . This is partly because damage to our DNA accumulates over time, activating enzymes that use up NAD+ more quickly. Another enzyme, called CD38, also becomes more active with age and inflammation, increasing NAD+ use. Meanwhile, our cells may become less efficient at producing it .
The extent of this decline varies between people and different tissues, with some studies suggesting that NAD+ levels may fall by between 10% and 80% as we age.
Lower NAD+ levels have been linked to reduced energy production in cells, slower DNA repair and other changes associated with ageing.
Animal studies suggest that increasing NAD+ levels may improve muscle function and metabolism and even cognitive function , encouraging researchers to investigate whether similar benefits are possible in humans.
There is limited evidence that taking NAD+ itself as a supplement effectively increases NAD+ levels, as it is broken down during digestion . A potential solution to this could be liposomal NAD+, where the molecule is enclosed in tiny fat-based structures designed to improve absorption.
A 2026 study involving 14 people found that taking 1,000mg of liposomal NAD+ daily for two weeks increased NAD+ levels inside cells by more than 64%. However, larger, carefully controlled studies are needed to confirm this finding.
Most human research has instead focused on NAD+ precursors: substances the body uses to make NAD+. These include two compounds derived from vitamin B3, nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN).
There is good evidence that both can increase NAD+ levels in the blood.
In one randomised, placebo-controlled study involving 140 overweight but otherwise healthy adults aged 40–60, NR supplementation increased blood NAD+ levels over eight weeks. The greatest increase occurred among those taking 1,000 mg (milligrams) daily, whose levels rose by 142% after two weeks and remained elevated throughout the study.
Another study involving 30 healthy adults found that taking 250 mg of NMN daily increased blood NAD+ levels by around 50% after four weeks, with levels remaining elevated throughout the 12-week trial.
High doses of vitamin B3 may also increase NAD+ , although these can be poorly tolerated over longer periods.
Together, these findings suggest that NAD+ precursors can successfully raise blood NAD+ levels. However, whether this also increases levels in other tissues, such as muscles and organs, remains unclear .
Animal studies have produced encouraging results, with NAD+ precursors improving physical performance, insulin sensitivity and the way cells produce energy . One study found that giving older mice NR for six weeks increased their lifespan by an average of 39 days , equivalent to around 5%.
However, results from human studies have been less convincing.
A recent systematic review examined 33 human studies and found inconsistent effects on physical function,

O9085d.title: Funding to help prevent workplace sexual harassment
O9085d.text:
Researchers at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) have secured almost £250,000 in Government funding to accelerate the development of a pioneering digital platform designed to help organisations prevent sexual harassment and sexual assault in the workplace before serious incidents occur.
The Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Auditing Service (SASHAS) has received UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) Proof of Concept funding to support its transition from a validated research prototype into a market-ready tool for organisations in the UK and internationally.
Developed by Professor Matt Fossey and Dr Ashley Perry at ARU, SASHAS is a comprehensive digital intelligence platform designed to measure and monitor workplace sexual harassment and sexual assault. It captures employee experiences and perceptions and transforms them into actionable insights through advanced analytics and real-time data visualisation.
By providing metrics at organisational, departmental, and team levels, SASHAS analyses data to identify where inappropriate behaviours are occurring and, crucially, highlights emerging risk areas before they escalate into more serious incidents.
Traditional reporting systems often rely on formal complaints being made after harm has already occurred. Instead, SASHAS is designed to help organisations recognise cultural vulnerabilities and warning signs earlier, allowing leaders to take preventative action and strengthen safeguarding measures.
The project comes amid heightened national attention on workplace culture. Research suggests that many incidents continue to go unreported because victims fear negative consequences or lack confidence in reporting processes.
SASHAS emerged from a NATO research programme examining sexual misconduct across militaries, where estimates suggest that military sexual trauma can affect over 20% of serving personnel. Researchers identified a need for tools capable of assessing not only incidents of misconduct, but also the organisational conditions that can allow harmful behaviours to occur and remain hidden.
Having been rigorously tested and piloted across multiple organisations, the platform is now entering its next phase of development. The new funding will support enhanced analytics, expanded user testing, readying for procurement and the development of sustainable commercial pathways for wider adoption.
“Sexual harassment and sexual assault are often understood through formal reports and investigations, but these only represent a fraction of what people experience. Organisations need better ways of understanding workplace culture, barriers to reporting, and emerging risks before harm escalates. SASHAS has been designed to provide that insight, helping organisations move from reactive responses towards prevention.”
“We are incredibly pleased that UKRI has recognised the potential of this work. SASHAS has emerged from years of research into organisational culture, safeguarding, and wellbeing. This funding will help us transform a validated research innovation into a practical tool that can support organisations, improve workplace safety, and strengthen trust in institutions.”
The research has been led by ARU’s Veterans and Families Institute for Military Social Research (VFI) in collaboration with the International Policing and Public Protection Research Institute (IPPPRI) and the Centre of Excellence for Equity in Uniformed Public Services (CEEUPS) .

Hello, and welcome to the October edition of our newsletter.
The last month has seen important developments in the future direction of regulation for both the rail and road sectors.
First, we saw the publication by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade of the independent review of the Office of Rail and Road led by Dr Richard Judge. The review recognises the value of our independence, expertise and unique role across economic and safety regulation. It also identifies opportunities to build on these strengths, many of which align with work already under way through our transformation programme.
Second, we saw the publication of the Highways (Financing) Bill which was laid in Parliament on 10 September. Once enacted this will enable us to take on the economic regulation for the Lower Thames Crossing (LTC) which will connect Kent and Essex through a tunnel beneath the River Thames.
With the importance of changes in the regulatory landscape – including for rail – I was delighted to speak at the Regulatory Policy Institute annual conference in Oxford earlier in September, sharing a panel with senior representatives from the rail freight sector and Network Rail.
As well as engaging with the regulatory and legislative changes afoot, we have also continued our important work of holding Network Rail to account. Just today, we have published reports on the economic and financial performance of Network Rail and on cost benchmarking .
Our analysis here shows how, despite above target efficiency performance, a number of factors have nevertheless led to overall cost increases. Network Rail delivered £614 million of efficiency improvements in the second year of CP7, covering April 2025 to March 2026, but inflationary pressures, maintenance of ageing assets and train performance issues placed additional pressure on Network Rail’s financial performance in the last year.
Another report featured this month is our 2026 open access monitoring report . This provides an update on open access passenger services, including an overview of new open access services and open access decisions; market outcomes since our 2025 report (such as punctuality, service growth and passenger experience); and a summary of what international market participants are saying.

We are delighted to have been able to bring forward improvements to the risk fee funds to support investors and improve service standards, while ensuring that risk is allocated appropriately and achieving value for money to enable further investment, ensuring the railway delivers the maximum economic benefit for the country.

O5faf8.title: Near 100-year-old gas pipes to be replaced in Elmstead Market
O5faf8.text:
Gas pipes that were first installed in Elmstead Market in the 1930s are to be upgraded to new, durable plastic pipes which will future-proof the network for decades to come.
Cadent is set to replace 320 metres of ageing gas pipe in Elmstead Market, helping to keep local homes and businesses connected to safe and reliable gas supplies for cooking and heating.
The works will take place in Church Road, from the junction of Holly Way to the junction of Colchester Road/Clacton Road. A road closure will be in place between these points to keep engineers and road users safe while the work is completed. Signed diversion routes and advance warning signs will be used where required.
The project is part of Cadent’s ongoing investment to upgrade older gas mains across the East of England, replacing ageing pipes with modern plastic ones that are more durable and ready for the future.
Following consultation with Essex County Council, Cadent has agreed to carry out these essential gas works starting on 17 August. The project is due to take six weeks to complete, with a permit in place until 21 September.
Eleanor Buxton, Head of Work Management at Cadent, said: The gas pipes in this part of Elmstead have been working hard for nearly 100 years, but it’s now time to replace them so we can continue to deliver gas safely and reliably to homes and businesses.
We know roadworks can be frustrating and we are sorry for any inconvenience caused. We will do all we can to keep disruption to a minimum and complete the work as safely and efficiently as possible.
This investment will help make sure the local gas network remains safe, reliable and ready to support the community for decades to come.
Gas supplies remain ON for the duration of work. The only interruption to supply will be to properties that take a direct feed from the pipes being replaced (in the immediate local area). Supply to these properties will be disconnected for a short while the property is connected to the new pipe. Advance notice will be given, and more information will be provided to these properties.
If you smell gas, always ring the National Gas Emergency Service immediately on 0800 111 999*, day or night. Do not assume it is related to this work; it may not be and needs to be checked.
Cadent is the UK’s largest gas distribution network with a 200-year legacy. We are in a unique position to build on strong foundations whilst encouraging the curiosity to think differently and the courage to embrace change. Day to day we continue to operate, maintain and innovate the UK’s largest gas network, transporting gas safely and protecting people in an emergency. Our skilled engineers and specialists remain committed to the communities we serve, working day and night to ensure gas reaches 11 million homes from Cumbria to North London and the Welsh Borders to East Anglia, to keep your energy flowing.
Here at Cadent we support the Government’s plans to reach Net Zero by 2050. That means we’re backing the introduction of hydrogen as a low carbon alternative to natural gas for the future. We know people love the controllability of gas and, with our network already in place, it makes sense to switch to the lower carbon alternative offered by hydrogen, which we believe can keep homes and businesses warm for generations to come.

While a temporary usage ban, often referred to as a hosepipe ban, is not currently being introduced, Essex & Suffolk Water is closely monitoring water resources and preparing for all eventualities.
Kieran Ingram, Water Director, said: " It takes a great deal of effort to turn rainwater into clean, safe drinkable water for everyday use, and the recent spell of hot, dry weather has led to a significant increase in water demand across Suffolk.
“Because of this, we need to formally appeal to our customers to show restraint with their water use and ask them to help us by considering how they use water.
"We're asking customers to help by using water wisely wherever possible. Small changes can make a big difference and could help reduce the likelihood of restrictions being needed later in the summer.
"We're continuing to tackle leaks and bursts and are doing everything we can to manage supplies, but we also need customers' help.
“If a temporary water use ban becomes necessary, we’ll work closely with local communities to provide the right support. But by making wise choices now, our customers can help lower the risk of such restrictions being needed.”
To try and help avoid any restrictions the water company is asking its customers in the Suffolk areas to consider using less water.

“There is a close relationship between rainfall, the amount of raw water available in our reservoirs and groundwater sources, and overall demand for water, including leakage and customer use.

Of4c23.title: How much does it need to rain before the temporary use hosepipe ban is lifted?
Of4c23.source: Northumbrian Water Group releases (Essex & Suffolk Water)
Of4c23.text:
There is no specific amount of rainfall that would allow the temporary use hosepipe ban to be lifted. Decisions are based on a range of factors, including reservoir levels, river flows, groundwater levels, soil moisture and the wider environmental impact of drought.
In Essex and Suffolk, rainfall in July was just 3% of the long-term average, and only 34% in August. The Environment Agency is also monitoring soil moisture, which shows the ground is currently around 30% drier than normal.
After months of hot and dry weather, the ground is very dry and compacted, meaning rainfall cannot easily soak into the soil. Steady, damp and prolonged rainfall conditions allow water to slowly soak into the ground, replenishing soil moisture and groundwater.
This recovery process typically takes place over autumn and winter. As rivers and groundwater recover, reservoirs can also begin to replenish, helping build water supplies for the following year.
While the recent rainfall has been welcome, sustained periods of wetter weather will be needed before drought conditions ease and restrictions can be reviewed.
Kieran Ingram, Water Director, said: “ After a prolonged period of hot and dry weather, the ground, rivers and groundwater sources all need time to recover. Recent rainfall has helped, but much more is needed before we see a significant improvement in water resources.
"Nature will take time to recover, and while the recent rainfall is encouraging, we will need sustained wetter weather over the coming months before drought conditions ease and restrictions can be reviewed."
Drought recovery happens in stages. Rainfall first needs to restore moisture levels in the soil, which have been depleted by months of hot and dry weather. Once the ground has recovered, water can more easily reach rivers and groundwater sources to enable the recovery of reservoir levels and a return to more normal water resource conditions.
Customers can help protect water resources by using less water at home and in the garden.
To find out how you can help nature, visit our website and use our water saving calculator for hints and tips on how to bring down your water usage: Save Water | How to Help With Water Conservation

O22130.title: Northumbrian Water Group achieves world first for customer service excellence
O22130.source: Northumbrian Water Group releases (Essex & Suffolk Water)
O22130.text:
The company, which operates in the North East as Northumbrian Water and in Essex and Suffolk as Essex & Suffolk Water, has been officially awarded the Service Excellence Kitemark™ by the British Standards Institution (BSI).
Recognising organisations that consistently put customers at the heart of everything they do, the independent assessment looked at how the company listens to customers, resolves problems and continually improves its services based on customer feedback.
It also considered the support it has available to customers who may need extra help, including through the company’s Priority Services Register and affordability schemes.
The achievement builds on Northumbrian Water Group’s existing BSI Kitemark™ for Inclusive Service, which it received in 2023 for its efforts supporting vulnerable customers across the region.
Northumbrian Water Group is now the first water company globally to hold both the Service Excellence and Inclusive Service Kitemarks™ together, and sees these external benchmarks as strong evidence of its ambition to provide world-class services to customers across its operating regions.
Together with its recently achieved Innovation Management Kitemark™, which measures practices for using innovation to deliver results for customers, communities, and environment, the latest certification means Northumbrian Water Group has also become the first organisation in the world, across any industry, to hold these three BSI Kitemarks™ at the same time.
The accreditations follow a strong track record in customer service, with Northumbrian Water Group ranking as the top performing water company in Ofwat's Customer Measure of Experience (C-MeX) for the past two years and recently being again named the most trusted water company in England and Wales.
Dawn Creighton, Head of Customer Strategy and Experience at Northumbrian Water Group, said: “Our customers are at the heart of everything we do, and we aim to deliver an unrivalled customer experience every single day, so this certification is something we're incredibly proud of.
"But it all starts with our people. We live and work in the communities we serve, and we all care about the services we provide because our customers are our friends, neighbours and family members too.
"We’re genuinely passionate about listening to our customers, understanding what's important to them and making sure it's as easy as possible for them to get the help and support they need.
"This achievement reflects the hard work and dedication of colleagues right across our business who go above and beyond every day to do the right thing for our customers."
The certifications recognise the company's commitment to delivering great customer service, making support accessible to all and continually improving the services it provides.
Shahm Barhom, Managing Director, Product Certification, BSI, said: "Putting customers first is more important than ever, and the Service Excellence Kitemark is a rigorous, independent benchmark for organisations that do this consistently well.
"Northumbrian Water Group's achievement in becoming the first water company in the world to gain this certification, and the first organisation globally to hold the Service Excellence, Inclusive Service and Innovation Management Kitemarks together, shows a genuine commitment to its customers and sets a strong example for the water sector."

Oa266c.title: Colchester gas pipes set for upgrade
Oa266c.text:
Ageing gas pipes are being replaced in Colchester by engineers from Cadent – the UK’s largest gas distribution network.
The project will see more than 950 metres of ageing gas pipes dating from the 1950s replaced in the bridleway that runs from Prettygate Road to Norman Way. The tough new pipes are designed to last for decades, helping to future-proof the local network.
Work gets underway on Monday 7 December, with permits in place until 4 January 2027.
Cadent has worked with Essex County Council to plan the essential work and minimise disruption as far as possible.
The pathway will be closed for the duration of the works to ensure the safety of engineers and the public.
A public event will be held between 2pm and 4pm on Monday 23 November in Norman Way, next to the car park for Colchester County High School for Girls. It is an opportunity for residents and businesses to learn more about the scheme and ask any questions. There is no need to book an appointment – just turn up and chat with a member of the team.
Gas stays ON for the duration of the works. The only interruption to supply will be to properties that take a direct feed from the pipes being replaced (in the immediate local area). Supply to these properties will be disconnected for a short while (it will be back on the same day it goes off), as the property gets connected into the new pipe. Advance notice will be given, and more information will be provided to these properties.
If you smell gas, always ring the National Gas Emergency Service immediately on 0800 111 999*, day or night. Do not assume it is related to these works; it may not be and needs to be checked.
Cadent is the UK’s largest gas distribution network with a 200-year legacy. We are in a unique position to build on strong foundations whilst encouraging the curiosity to think differently and the courage to embrace change. Day to day we continue to operate, maintain and innovate the UK’s largest gas network, transporting gas safely and protecting people in an emergency. Our skilled engineers and specialists remain committed to the communities we serve, working day and night to ensure gas reaches 11 million homes from Cumbria to North London and the Welsh Borders to East Anglia, to keep your energy flowing.
Here at Cadent we support the Government’s plans to reach Net Zero by 2050. That means we’re backing the introduction of hydrogen as a low carbon alternative to natural gas for the future. We know people love the controllability of gas and, with our network already in place, it makes sense to switch to the lower carbon alternative offered by hydrogen, which we believe can keep homes and businesses warm for generations to come.

Ofdc07.title: Ceremony sees new ARU Chancellor formally invested
Ofdc07.text:
ARU's new Chancellor Professor Lady Sue Black
The formal investiture of Professor Lady Sue Black as the new Chancellor of Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) took place this week during graduation celebrations for hundreds of students in Chelmsford.
One of the world's leading forensic scientists, Professor Lady Black is an internationally respected academic, author and public servant whose career has been distinguished by excellence in education, research and civic contribution.
Since graduating from the University of Aberdeen in Human Anatomy, Professor Lady Black has made an exceptional contribution to forensic science. Her work for the UK Government and international agencies has taken her across the world, including investigations in Iraq, Sierra Leone and Grenada, and she served as lead forensic anthropologist during the international war crimes investigations in Kosovo.
Alongside her academic achievements, she has been recognised through numerous honours, including her appointment as Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 2016, election as a Fellow of the Royal Society in 2023, appointment to the Most Ancient and Most Noble Order of the Thistle in 2024, and her service as a Crossbench member of the House of Lords.
Professor Lady Black is currently the 37th President of St John's College, Oxford, and previously served as Pro Vice Chancellor for Engagement at Lancaster University.
Among her many media appearances, Professor Lady Black has featured as the guest on The Life Scientific and Desert Island Discs on BBC Radio 4. She is also the author of three books, the most recent of which, An Expert Witness , was published in July.
ARU’s autumn graduation ceremonies in Chelmsford, Cambridge and Peterborough this month will see 3,140 students formally receive their degrees, ready to take the next step in their lives.
“It is a tremendous honour to stand before you today as the new Chancellor of Anglia Ruskin University. I feel enormously privileged to be taking on this role and I do so with a genuine sense of excitement, humility and I hope a healthy dose of Scottish Highland determination.
“Universities have always held a special place in my heart. They are extraordinary places full of extraordinary people. They are where curiosity is encouraged, where conventional thinking can be challenged, where ideas are born, and where people are given the opportunity to discover not only what they can achieve, but who they might become.”
“Professor Lady Sue Black is a passionate advocate for widening opportunity through education and for ensuring that universities make a meaningful contribution to the communities they serve. In accepting her appointment as Chancellor, she spoke of her commitment to supporting and championing Anglia Ruskin University's work across research, education and civic engagement, and of the importance she places on transforming lives and widening opportunity through social mobility.
“Her values, her commitment to public service, and her belief in the power of education align closely with the mission of Anglia Ruskin University: transforming lives through innovative, inclusive and entrepreneurial education and research.”

O1c187.title: Christmas gifts and festive fun at unique ARU market
O1c187.text:
Students at last year's Elevate Winter Market. Photo courtesy of Richard Howell Photography
Christmas shoppers will be able to pick up unique festive gifts, enjoy seasonal treats and try their hand at a range of games and activities when Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) students bring their annual Elevate Winter Market to Cambridge and Chelmsford next month.
The free event, open to the public, will take place on Tuesday, 1 December in the Helmore and Lord Ashcroft buildings at ARU's Cambridge campus on East Road, before moving on to the Michael Ashcroft building at ARU's Chelmsford campus on Thursday, 3 December, with shoppers invited to browse stalls created and run by student entrepreneurs.

After pitching for seed funding and creating their festive ventures, students will be selling directly to members of the public while supporting charities across the local community.
Last year’s market raised around £2,000 for good causes and this year the aim is to double that, with proceeds to be shared around charities and organisations including Jimmy's Cambridge, Little Miracles, Red2Green, The Craig Tyler Trust, Streets2Homes, MIND in West Essex and Trust Links.

O8812c.title: Identical twins ready to deliver after graduation joy
O8812c.text:
Twin sisters Freya Ward, pictured left, and Ella Ward at their ARU graduation ceremony in Chelmsford
Two identical twin sisters are ready to deliver after graduating from the Midwifery course at Anglia Ruskin University (ARU).
Ella and Freya Ward, from Benfleet, have journeyed together through school, college and university and will now go on to work as midwives at Basildon Hospital after graduating at Chelmsford Cathedral this week.
The 21-year-olds attended Appleton School in Benfleet before going to nearby USP College to study health and social care. They then applied to ARU where they both underwent hospital placements at Basildon Hospital.
They even passed their driving tests three days apart, and for a while shared a car to travel into university and to placements.
Freya said: “We’re very similar in lots of ways. We share the same friends and the same interests. We both liked the idea of becoming midwives so it seemed a natural path to take for us both.
“My mum was the person who first gave me the idea to become a midwife when I was 15, and I have never looked back since. My parents and wider family have been amazing throughout my training and have always been there to encourage me during moments when I doubted my abilities.”
While going through life together as identical twins has been fairly seamless, the situation has sometimes thrown up unusual challenges for others.
Freya added: “One of the most memorable moments was on the delivery suite when Ella had finished a day shift and I had just started the night shift. A patient I was caring for asked if I was feeling alright after such a long day. I immediately realised she had mistaken me for my sister and had to explain I'd only arrived a few hours earlier. We all laughed and it became a bit of a joke among the midwives.”
Ella said: “We’re used to it but we do get quite a lot of people interested in how it works and asking us questions. They usually want to know who has delivered the most babies, or whether the patients and other midwives get confused.”
Their hospital placements also confirmed they had chosen the right profession. Both sisters vividly remember delivering their first babies during her first year of training.
Remembering that first delivery, Freya said: “I was lucky enough to be working with an amazing midwife who took the time to explain things to me and made me feel included in the experience. It is a really nice memory and reminds me that even throughout the busy, more stressful moments, birth can be calm and empowering. I will always remember and be grateful to that family.”
Ella said: “I remember being excited about the first birth. An amazing midwife helped me deliver the baby and they called the baby Freya which I thought was funny and obviously I told my sister straight away!”
Although the similarities between Ella and Freya are clear, they both had different strengths while studying.
Ella added: “I was stronger with coursework and Freya was better with exams. When it came to revising for exams, Freya helped me with revision notes and preparation for those. Everyone has those high and low moments but we helped each other through.”

O68a97.title: Seven historic buildings we’re funding to become community hubs
O68a97.text:
We’ve awarded grants to over 300 projects since 1994 that have transformed historic buildings and natural heritage spaces into dedicated hubs for public activities supporting learning, training and wellbeing.
Our local teams fund communities to restore and reuse the historic places that matter to them, and achieve their potential to make a difference to people's lives and local economies.
Community hubs provide social, mental health and shared learning benefits for all and, critically, give new life to formerly redundant buildings.
Eilish McGuinness, Chief Executive of The National Lottery Heritage Fund
Our £402,000 grant is supporting plans to reinvigorate a community hub and wayfinding centre for visitors that will share the history of the Essex town. Shoeburyness was used for testing guns and ammunition for the army and navy from 1850 and as a military base during both world wars. It’s also where dogs were trained as messengers, sentries and for patrolling there during the First World War.
Two 18th-century buildings on the high street of this coastal town are being restored and refurbished as part of an expansion of its community-focused local museum. Dr Nic Wright from the project spoke to us recently about overcoming challenges and how on-the-ground engagement has created a buzz in the town for the £2.1m project.
This Georgian building is already a valued centre for delivering community services across Kendal, Westmorland and Furness. Our £4.6m grant will restore the building and upgrade its accessibility so it can better serve local charitable, voluntary and community sector needs.
Activities benefitting local people will be at the heart of the project, following conservation and enhancement of this unusually grand place of worship in rural Norfolk, thanks to our £475,000 grant. Working with HoltYouth Project, which serves around 200 local young people, the project will run cookery lessons and provide respite meals for young carers.
Our grant of £2.65m starts a new chapter in the 1,000-year history of Colchester’s oldest building. Urgent conservation will remove the Grade I listed building from Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register and repurpose it as a welcoming community space open daily to the public for the first time since 2017.
Our £1.2m funding will help refurbish and expand this centre – which tells the story of the people of the Outer Hebrides – and support more family tree and heritage research and Gaelic language learning.
We’ve awarded Bolton Council and Lancashire Wildlife Trust £4.4m to renovate this derelict Grade II listed historic building. It’ll be turned into a centre for celebrating local heritage through creative interpretation, exhibitions and event programming.
By restoring the old rather than building new, these projects will have a lower environmental impact and support traditional heritage skills while retaining the individual character of their areas, neighbourhoods or towns. And as useful spaces for local people and visitors to learn and have fun, they will help people connect with each other and the past.
Eilish McGuinness, Chief Executive of The National Lottery Heritage Fund, said: “Heritage has a unique role in building pride in place and connection to the past, bringing people together where they live, work and visit.
“Community hubs provide social, mental health and shared learning benefits for all and, critically, give new life to formerly redundant buildings.”

O5e097.title: Hartismere homes make the move to smart meters
O5e097.source: Northumbrian Water Group releases (Essex & Suffolk Water)
O5e097.text:
The milestone comes as Essex & Suffolk Water continues its smart metering programme across the area, helping customers use water more efficiently and protect local resources for the future.
Now, the water firm’s community engagement team is heading out across the area to meet customers face-to-face, answer any questions about the smart metering programme and share practical water-saving advice.
The team will be holding a series of local sessions at village halls and community spaces, many of them alongside the Rural Coffee Caravan, a free service that helps rurally isolated people in Suffolk access services and information.
Happening throughout November and December, customers will be able to drop in for a chat over a cup of tea or coffee, find out more about smart meters and pick up simple tips to help reduce water use at home.
Smart meters send readings to Essex & Suffolk Water automatically which customers can keep track of, helping them to understand how much water they use and highlighting changes in usage that could indicate a leak.
This can help households avoid wasting water and identify problems sooner, saving money on bills in the process.
Since the hosepipe ban began in August, households on a smart meter in Hartismere, have saved 64 litres of water per day – equivalent to about five large buckets full of water - helping to reduce demand on local water supplies.
Dominic Butcher, Head of Metering at Essex & Suffolk Water, said: "Most customers in Hartismere have already made the move to smart metering and we’re really grateful to customers for their support as the programme continues.
"For many people, seeing their water use can help them spot simple ways to save water, which is good for both the environment and their household budget too.
"We know some people still have questions about smart meters, so these community events are a great opportunity to come along, meet the team and find out more about metering and water-saving.”

O92eb8.text:
Chelmsford City are delighted to announce the signing of midfielder Jack Roles from National League North side South Shields.
The 27-year-old brings experience from across the Football League and the National League. Roles came through the academy at Tottenham Hotspur, where he progressed through the youth ranks and featured for the first team against Juventus in pre-season. Roles got his first taste of senior football on loan at Cambridge United in 2019. He scored five goals in 23 League Two appearances and was named the division’s Player of the Month in October, with one of his long-range strikes also nominated for Goal of the Month. Further loan spells with Burton Albion and Stevenage followed before he joined Crystal Palace and later moved to Woking.
The midfielder joined Crawley Town from Woking in January 2023 and went on to make 91 appearances for the Red Devils. He helped Crawley win promotion to League One in 2024, scoring a volley in the play-off semi-final second leg against MK Dons as they booked their place at Wembley. Roles went on to make 20 appearances in League One the following season.
Roles also spent time on loan at Gateshead before signing for South Shields in February 2026. He now makes the move to Chelmsford City.

Ob4503.text:
Free health checks, a flu vaccination drop-in for eligible people and opportunities to take part in health research are being offered to Clacton residents at a free event on Monday (30 November).
Organised by NHS Essex, the Research, Health and Wellbeing event will take place at Clacton Leisure Centre from 12.30pm to 3.30pm, bringing together NHS services, researchers and local community organisations under one roof.
A wide range of local organisations will be attending, offering information on healthy lifestyles, mental health, community wellbeing and support services. Residents will have the chance to speak directly to health professionals, ask questions and find out more about the support available in their local area.
During the event, visitors will be able to:
access free health checks, including blood pressure and cholesterol checks
receive advice and support to help them look after their health and wellbeing
Get their free flu vaccinations if they are eligible, including children aged two and three, giving families an opportunity to protect their little ones against flu this winter.
Find out how health research is helping improve healthcare for the future.
Get involved in research including Be Part of Research, Improving Black Health Outcomes, Genes & Health and the DNA, Children + Young People’s Health Resource (D-CYPHR).
As part of the event Professor Andrew Bateman from the University of Essex will be showcasing a Parkinson’s research study using augmented reality headsets, giving residents a chance to see how technology is being explored in health research.
Parents and carers can also find out more about protecting their children against common winter illnesses through NHS Essex’s Super Bodies campaign .
Event details
Date: Monday 30 November 2026
Time: 12.30pm to 3.30pm
Location: Clacton Leisure Centre, Vista Road, Clacton-on-Sea, CO15 6DJ

As the firm grows, we must keep listening to our people and building an environment where everyone feels valued, supported and able to do their best work.

I am proud of our employee engagement and, as Price Bailey continues to grow, I remain committed to ensuring that we will always be an outstanding company to work for.”
The firm has implemented several innovative policies based on employee feedback over the last decade, including Smart Working. Smart Working offers a flexible working arrangement for all staff, allowing Price Bailey people to work at times that best suit them, their clients and the firm. They also offer a ‘dress for your day’ policy, promoting a comfortable, modern, yet professional experience for employees and clients. O8670e.text:
Epping Forest District Council’s Cabinet has approved a new Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy, backed plans to invest in technology to support customer services and considered a range of governance and financial reports.
Opening the meeting, the Leader of the Council, Cllr Chris Whitbread, addressed concerns regarding the rejection of public questions relating to Qualis Commercial. He reaffirmed the Council’s commitment to transparency and effective scrutiny, explaining that the Council’s Constitution contains provisions designed to avoid substantial duplication of issues already considered through public meetings, and to ensure Council business remains focused on matters requiring consideration and decision.
View the agenda for Cabinet 26 November
Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy
At its meeting on 26 November 2026, Cabinet approved a new Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy 2026-2031.
The strategy sets out how the Council, and its partners will work together over the next five years to prevent homelessness, tackle rough sleeping and improve housing outcomes for residents.
Demand for homelessness support has increased in recent years, with approaches to the Council rising from 1,086 households in 2022/23 to 1,357 in 2025/26. The strategy focuses on early intervention, partnership working and increasing access to suitable accommodation to help residents at risk of homelessness.
Customer Services technology
Cabinet also approved plans to invest in a new enterprise communications platform. The technology is intended to support future improvements to customer service and help create a more joined-up experience for residents when contacting the Council.
While digital tools will play an important role in supporting services in the future, the Council remains committed to ensuring residents can access help in the way that works best for them, including through personal support and non-digital channels.
Other business
Cabinet also considered a range of governance and financial reports, including budget monitoring, risk management, and an updated debt recovery policy.

O5adfb.title: When Christmas brings heartbreak: New Essex business launches to help people navigate separation
O5adfb.text:
After experiencing the breakdown of her own 21-year relationship just weeks before Christmas, Clacton based Ann Scott is turning personal experience into practical support for others facing separation.
Christmas is often portrayed as a time of family, happiness and togetherness. But for people facing the end of a relationship, it can be one of the loneliest and most difficult times of the year.
While the world seems to be preparing to celebrate, some people are quietly facing the prospect of a very different future. Questions about where they will live, how they will manage financially and how they begin again can feel impossible to answer.
It is against this backdrop that Essex entrepreneur Ann Scott is launching The Ember Path ; a separation navigation service designed to help people make sense of the practical realities of relationship breakdown with clarity, confidence and support.
The service is for people across Essex, married or unmarried, whether they are the person initiating the separation or the one coming to terms with it.
For Ann, this is far more than a business idea. It comes from a place of deeply personal experience.
“Less than two weeks before Christmas, I was faced with the devastating blow of discovering infidelity in my 21-year relationship. That, in itself, is hard to process, but then comes the realisation that the future you had planned is gone in just one conversation.
“When your partner of over two decades tells you that someone significantly younger that he’s known for just two months and her children are now his priority, it’s certainly a shock. Even more so when you learn they are planning to move them into your home! It felt like jumping out a plane – not only are you winded by the rush of air to your chest but you have no idea where you will land.
“While other people were thinking about presents, celebrations and family gatherings, I was facing a future I didn’t want and had never planned for. I had a seemingly endless list of practical questions and decisions to make; it was overwhelming as I didn’t know where to start and who I could trust or afford for advice.
“Thankfully, I work with small businesses across Essex in my full-time employment and had a network of trusted connections at my fingertips. They were able to guide and signpost me, so I felt more confident in the decisions I was making”.
It was this experience that planted the seed for Ann’s business.
Separation is one of the most stressful and financially consequential experiences a person can face. Yet while solicitors guide people through the legal process and therapists help them deal with their emotions, there is often a huge gap between the two.
That gap is where The Ember Path sits.
What paperwork needs completing? How do you separate your finances? What happens to the mortgage? What decisions need to be made about the family home? Who should you speak to, and in what order?
The Ember Path helps people make sense of these questions, breaking an overwhelming situation into manageable steps and introducing them to trusted professionals; including solicitors, mortgage brokers and conveyancers. Accessing the right support at the right time is vital, particularly when stress can cloud judgement and decisions can have lifelong consequences.
“This isn’t about someone telling you how to feel or what decisions to make, as every situation is unique and only you will know what feels right. But I know how important it is to have someone to help you understand the options available and get specialist advice.

Chelmsford City FC – A New Structure for an Exciting Future
Since taking over Chelmsford City Football Club, our ambition has always been clear: to build a successful and ambitious football club that our supporters, our community and our city can be proud of.
We’ve made significant progress over the past few years, both on and off the pitch. Attendances have grown, we’ve strengthened the club commercially, invested in our infrastructure and taken the important step towards becoming a full-time football club. But as I’ve said many times before,  better never stops.
If we’re serious about achieving our ambitions, which we are, we must continue to evolve, improve and put the right people and structures in place to take us to the next level. With that in mind, I’m pleased to announce a number of changes to the leadership and management structure of Chelmsford City FC.

O80d4a.title: Father and Son Cycle 500km From Plymouth to Southend-on-Sea in Aid of Local Hospice Care
O80d4a.text:
A father and son have cycled 500km from Plymouth to Fair Havens adults’ hospice in Southend-on-Sea, raising over £4,000 in memory of their father-in-law and grandfather, Paul Wellsteed.
James (45) and Ted Warne (17) arrived at Fair Havens on 31st October after six gruelling days cycling from their home in Noss Mayo, a village near Plymouth.
The pair began their journey after the passing of Storms Austen and Boelo and faced mixed weather conditions, from heavy rain to misty mornings. They cycled around 80km per day and, after three days, took a day off to rest when they both fell ill. Despite the difficult setback, they continued to push on for a further three days and were welcomed at Fair Havens by family, close friends, and staff.
James has previously completed the London to Southend bike ride, but for Ted, this was his first long-distance cycling experience, making the achievement even greater.
Paul sadly died from stage four bile-duct cancer in June, having been cared for by Fair Havens. The money his son-in-law and grandson have raised will help Havens Hospices continue giving expert, compassionate care to people of all ages living with incurable conditions, and to families just like theirs.
When reflecting upon their experience, James said, “Ted and I decided to do this ride after seeing Grandad being cared for at Fair Havens. We wanted to take on a challenge in his memory, while also giving back to the hospice that cared for him and our family.
“We moved to Devon eight years ago from Leigh-on-Sea and it felt like a good idea to cycle from our new home to our old home.
“Spending quality time with Ted, taking in the scenery and seeing my wife, Amy, waiting for us at the end of three very long, difficult days – these are memories I’ll always remember.”
Susie May, Fundraising Officer at Havens Hospices, said, “All of our care and support is provided free of charge, and that’s only possible because of generous people like James and Ted. Cycling 500km in memory of Paul is a remarkable thing to do, and we’re so grateful they chose to support Havens Hospices in his memory.”
To support James and Ted’s cycling challenge, visit their JustGiving page: www.justgiving.com/page/tedandjamesplymouthtosouthend

O50950.title: Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No. 2) Bill | Commons debates
O50950.text:
The law exists to uphold our rights and freedoms and to protect the public interest, but the law can be used by bad actors against the public interest. As we have heard today, some use legal action or the threat of it to silence, exhaust and bankrupt their critics, who seek to expose their wrongdoing. We have heard powerful testimonies relayed by the Chair of the Justice Committee, my hon. Friend the Member for Derby North (Catherine Atkinson) , from victims who have been shamefully silenced, shut down and financially ruined when they have sought to speak out. Strategic lawsuits against public participation—SLAPPs—use the law in bad faith, and the private Member’s Bill before us would make it much harder to bring such suits.
I am very pleased that this important Bill, brought forward by my fellow Essex MP, the right hon. Member for Maldon (Sir John Whittingdale) , has received Government support. The right hon. Gentleman is extremely well placed to lead on these matters, given his long experience of speaking out on them. As a Minister and as the Chair of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, he played a pivotal part in exposing the phone-hacking scandals of the early 2000s and challenging those who sought to use legal means to conceal them, and I pay tribute to him.
The Bill will tackle SLAPPs and provide effective protections for defendants where such claims are still raised. It will help to reduce exposure to disproportionate legal costs, allow early dismissal of cases and prevent litigation from being used as a tool of delay, pressure or intimidation. By doing that, it will rebalance a system that is currently stacked in favour of those with wealth and power, and empower those who lack both.
This Bill will also strengthen the rule of good law in the UK and further afield. The right hon. Member for Maldon and I have shared commitments that stretch beyond Essex; we are both involved in the Inter Parliamentary Union, a body that seeks to spread good parliamentary practice at a global level. Through its co-operation with UNESCO on freedom of expression and digital governance, the IPU has hosted events examining the misuse of the judicial system to attack freedom of expression, including defamation laws and SLAPPs, and has made recommendations to legislators to reform defamation laws and protect journalists and parliamentarians from retaliatory legal pressure.

Od22a4.title: Record-breaking £26,000 raised for Royal British Legion Poppy Appeal
Od22a4.text:
More than £26,000 has been raised for the Royal British Legion at London Stansted after another hugely successful Poppy Appeal campaign.
A total of £26,190 was donated by passengers, airport colleagues and visitors, making it the biggest amount ever collected through the airport's annual appeal and more than £2,000 higher than last year's record-breaking total.
The achievement was made possible by a dedicated team of volunteers who gave up their time to support the appeal in the run-up to Remembrance Sunday.
In total, volunteers covered 148 three-hour shifts, with a further 64 shifts completed by members of the 33 and 35 Royal Engineer Regiments.
Simon Bambridge, Royal British Legion's Poppy Appeal organiser said:
"To raise more than £26,000 this year is an incredible achievement and I can't thank our volunteers, airport staff and passengers enough for their generosity and support. This appeal is only successful because so many people are willing to give up their time and contribute to such an important cause. Every donation will help the Royal British Legion continue its vital work supporting veterans and their families. For anyone who would like to volunteer for next years appeal, please do get in touch.”
Dan Turpin, Community Engagement Manager at London Stansted, said:
"The Poppy Appeal is an important part of life at London Stansted and it's something colleagues and passengers continue to get behind year after year. We're proud to support the Royal British Legion and delighted to see another record-breaking total. The money raised will help the charity continue the vital support it provides to serving personnel, veterans and their families."

O734ae.text:
Brentwood Town Football Club are delighted to announce the addition of Jay Lovett to Brett Munyard’s management team, with Jay taking up the role of First-Team Coach.
Jay arrives at The Arena with a wealth of experience across non-league football, having enjoyed a lengthy playing career before progressing into coaching and management.
As a player, Jay represented a number of clubs across the non-league pyramid, including Crawley Town, Brentford, Eastbourne Borough, Lewes and Whitehawk.
His playing career also saw him experience promotion success, helping Eastbourne Borough secure promotion to the Conference National via the Conference South play-offs in the 2007/08 season.
Following his transition into coaching, Jay spent four years working as a Youth Development Phase Coach at Brighton & Hove Albion, gaining valuable experience in player development before moving into senior management.
He has since held a number of positions across the non-league game, including spells with South Park, Burgess Hill Town and Haywards Heath Town, alongside coaching opportunities at Eastbourne Borough.
One of the highlights of his managerial career came during his second spell at Burgess Hill Town, where he returned in May 2024 as joint-manager alongside Gary Mansell.
The pair enjoyed a successful 2024/25 campaign, guiding Burgess Hill Town to promotion and further underlining Jay’s experience of building competitive sides and achieving success at this level.
More recently, Jay took charge of Whitehawk in the Isthmian Premier Division, before stepping down from the managerial role in October.
He now joins Brett and the rest of the coaching staff as the Blues continue to strengthen their first-team setup.
Everyone at Brentwood Town would like to warmly welcome Jay to the Club and wish him every success in his new role at The Arena.
