O586cc.title: Neighbourhood officers and council team up for fly tipping crackdown
O586cc.text:
Neighbourhood officers and council team up for fly tipping crackdown
Leona.Murraygreen
Date
26 November 2026
Date
26 November 2026
Category
Environment
Brentwood Neighbourhood Policing Team and Brentwood Borough Council’s environmental officers are fighting back against fly tippers as part of a new operation.
The joint team is carrying out extra patrols in areas of the borough that have been affected by the illegal dumping of waste and pulling over vans for spot checks.
Domestic waste, car parts and even burnt-out vehicles have been found by the roadside, and there have been occasions where roads have been blocked by building waste.
The officers believe the secluded areas of the borough, particularly in and around Navestock, have been targeted because of their close proximity to the M25 and A12.
PC Tom Marriott of Brentwood Neighbourhood Policing Team is leading the policing side of the operation and said that he understands the concerns of local residents:
“Fly tipping causes huge amounts of disruption and damages the environment.  We have seen examples of fly tips blocking entire country lanes, leaving a trail of rubbish that takes a long time to clear, impacting everyone living locally.
“A lot of the waste is household or building waste but we have also had people dumping hazardous materials like asbestos – materials that cost the council thousands to pick up and can harm people and wildlife.
“We’re here to help the council stop fly tipping and deter those people who think it’s OK to use the district to dump waste.
“If you’re getting rid of waste, be careful about who you’re passing it to. Make sure they’re an accredited company with a waste carrier licence, which can be checked on the Environment Agency website .
“If you see an active fly tip, call 999 and we’ll try to get to it. If you spot waste, use the What3Words app to tell us the exact location, take a picture and report it to the council.”
Councillor David Worsfold, Chair of Brentwood Borough Council’s Clean & Green Committee, added: “There are an average of three fly tips every day in the borough, and it costs more than £95,000 a year for their clearing and disposal. Working together with other agencies, like Essex Police, is important to tackle the issue.
“The Council uses fixed penalty notices in addition to the existing powers of prosecution to provide additional means of enforcement.
“We recently had a successful prosecution that resulted in a prison sentence which is a stark warning that if you are found guilty of fly-tipping in Brentwood, you could face imprisonment or a fine of up to £50,000.”

O5c261.title: Housing Targets and Green Belt: Castle Point | Commons debates
O5c261.source: Rebecca Harris MP (Castle Point) in Parliament
O5c261.text:
Absolutely—100%. Housing targets do not mean that houses get built automatically. They may be built, or we may just be planning a large number of sites on a map. If we build the level of housing being asked for in Castle Point on the sites that are potentially available to us, I do not think that many people will want to live there in 20 years’ time, because they will not be able to get anywhere. It will not make sense. We cannot build extra road capacity there—it is just not an option. Well, there is one place where we could do so, but I will come to that later.
I extend an offer to the Minister to visit my constituency, although I fear that he may not be comfortable with coming to Castle Point due to the live local plan. If he did, he could sit in traffic with me and explain how he thinks our road network will accommodate the residents of nearly 12,000 new homes. We would have ample time to discuss it, because we would be stuck in congestion.
The Government’s formula can produce a housing number, but it cannot widen the A13, create another route off Canvey or add capacity to our antiquated drainage network. Those are real-world problems that my constituents have to live with. Castle Point borough council’s own evidence to the examination says that, even with its lower proposed figure of 6,196 homes and the proposed mitigation measures, the traffic conditions will dramatically worsen. The council expects capacity to be exceeded on Canvey Way, parts of the A13, the A129 and roads on Canvey itself.
In August, the chief executive of Essex county council wrote to me to confirm that the highways authority had not yet received the revised transport assessment that it needed to satisfy itself that even those 6,196 homes could be accommodated in terms of capacity and, critically, safety, yet my council is being pressured to accommodate thousands more. Before deciding how many more houses Castle Point can take, surely somebody should establish whether our roads can safely take the traffic. The economic impact of the current levels of congestion should be enough of an argument on its own to reduce the number of houses in the Government’s target.
Of course, the traffic does not stop at the borough boundary. Our neighbouring authorities are also being asked to accommodate an enormous amount of development. Many residents in those new developments will use exactly the same stretches of road and exactly the same junctions as my constituents. The Minister cannot reasonably expect councils to plan for thousands of additional homes in isolation from one another, given that they all rely on the same incredibly overstretched infrastructure along the Thames estuary.
I am particularly concerned about the infrastructure on Canvey Island, which is home to 40,000 people. It is a strong and proud community, but it faces circumstances that very few other communities in this country have to contend with; indeed, I would say it is absolutely unique. Much of the island lies below sea level. It relies on extensive sea defences and a very complex network of pumps, ditches, culverts and drainage channels. The island has two roads to the mainland, both of which start at the same roundabout and then feed into the same heavily congested wider road network.
Canvey Island is also home to major industrial installations, including two top-tier control of major accident hazard sites, subject to stringent safety regulations, that are part of our national critical infrastructure. If the gas, and road and jet fuel, cannot leave the island because of traffic or an accident—one year, a tanker burst into flames, closing a road—it will have a genuinely wider impact on the energy resilience of the whole south-east of England and beyond. That has not received anywhere near enough consideration by the Government and has possibly been overlooked by the inspector, as he waded through reams of evidence.

A message from Eden, our Volunteer Co-ordinator
Last week I headed along to Thurrock Cares’ Warm Up for Winter event, this time hosted at Tilbury Community Association.
Services, charities and organisations of every kind had turned up for Tilbury residents, and the place was busy from start to finish. The conversations were the best part. Some were practical, some were emotional, and plenty of them were exactly the kind that needed to happen. That’s what these events do so well: they put the right people in the same room and let things follow.
I always love attending them. For me, it’s a chance to catch up with people who volunteer right now, to hear from those who’ve volunteered in the past (and some of the stories they have to tell are brilliant), and to talk to anyone who’s simply curious about what volunteering could look like for them.
And that’s really the point. You don’t have to wait for an outreach event to find me. If you’d like to gain new skills, give something back to your community, or make some new friends along the way, I’m always happy to have a chat.
How to get in touch
Call: 01375 389853
Email: volunteercentre@thurrockcvs.org
Or book an appointment with me at the Beehive Centre, or at a local library or community hub – wherever suits you best.

O70998.title: Preparing for winter: how the NHS is helping you stay well and cared for
O70998.text:
Michelle Stapleton, Winter Lead Director at NHS Essex explains how the NHS will ensure patients continue to get the care and support they need throughout the busy winter months.
Winter can be a worrying time for people who need care and for those looking after a loved one. When you are unwell, you want to know where to turn and that help will be there.
Local winter preparations focus on three things: helping you stay well, making it easier to get care and supporting you to return home safely after a hospital stay. As the lead for winter at NHS Essex, my role is to help make sure our services and partners are prepared to deliver that support, and that we respond together when pressures rise.
More people tend to need help during the colder months, and seasonal illnesses add to the pressure on busy services. While we cannot remove every difficulty, but we can plan ahead and work together to make the best use of the staff and services we have.
One shared plan
Preparing for winter is not just a job for hospitals. GP practices, ambulance crews, community and mental health services, local councils, social care teams and voluntary organisations all have a part to play.
Across Essex, we have a shared winter plan to bring that work together. We are keeping a daily view of demand and available care, so we can spot problems early and coordinate support where it is needed. That means looking beyond one service to understand how pressures in one place affect others.
The plan includes coordination seven days a week and clear arrangements for services to request additional support and help one another when pressures increase. This means our preparations are not just about assessing demand on services, they also set out how we respond together to protect patient safety.
By working together, we can arrange the care people need to return home safely when they are ready to leave hospital. That also frees up a bed for someone else who needs hospital care. If you can help a loved one who is ready to leave hospital, please speak with the ward team about practical support. This could be arranging a lift and making sure keys, food and heating are ready for when they get home so they can focus on their recovery. Let the ward team know about any concerns or support you cannot provide.
Working together also means that getting the right help early may prevent someone from needing to go into hospital in the first place.
We are also planning for changes in demand and supporting our workforce. Safe care depends on having the right people available, as well as looking after the staff who deliver it.
8,000 extra appointments in GP practices each month
To help meet increased winter demand, NHS Essex has invested £1.1 million in an additional 8,000 GP appointments each month from November 2026 to February 2027. We know how much being able to get an appointment at your GP practice matters, and this investment is intended to help more residents access care during winter.
That is 32,000 extra appointments over the four months, giving more people the opportunity to receive care close to home during the busiest time of year.
Depending on the care you need, these appointments may be with a GP or another member of the practice team, such as a nurse or physiotherapist. They will be delivered through participating groups of GP practices across Essex, including Southend and Thurrock.
This investment is an important part of our winter preparations. It will help increase access, although it does not mean we can promise that every pressure on local services will disappear.
More support closer to home
Across England, the government announced a £40 million programme on 9 November to help GP teams give extra support to people most at risk of becoming seriously unwell this winter.

Oe3712.title: Chelmsford family’s tribute to the hospice that helped them make memories with baby son
Oe3712.text:
A Chelmsford couple whose baby son died at Little Havens when he was just 36 days old are sharing their story to ensure other families have the same chance to make those precious memories together.
Michael and Sarah Fragnito’s son Elio spent the last two days of his life at Little Havens, the children’s hospice run by Havens Hospices. Now, the couple are supporting the hospice’s ‘Big “Yes!” Christmas Appeal’ so that other families have the same chance to hear “yes” when it matters most.
The idea behind its Big Yes! appeal is simple: the hospice’s nurses can only say “Yes!” to the people they care for if the community says “Yes!” to Havens Hospices.
“Our son Elio was just 36 days old when he died, peacefully in our arms at Little Havens,” they said. “Grief is awful, but love comes out on top. And Little Havens gave us the chance to fill Elio’s life with love.”
Elio was born after a straightforward pregnancy. “He was perfect,” said Michael and Sarah. “Everything felt normal.”
But within 36 hours, Elio became critically unwell. He was rushed into intensive care and then transferred to Great Ormond Street Hospital, where doctors found he had a rare and serious heart condition that hadn’t been picked up during pregnancy.
“The weeks that followed were filled with uncertainty, operations and hope that rose and fell daily,” they said. “For much of that time, we couldn’t hold him because he was connected to so many wires and machines. When we were finally able to cuddle our son again, it meant everything.”
Eventually, the family were told nothing more could be done, and Elio’s care would focus on keeping him comfortable. They were offered a choice: to stay in hospital, try to take him home, or go to Little Havens.
“At first, we didn’t want to go to a hospice. We wanted him at home. His bedroom was ready for him,” they said. “But we also knew what was coming. When we visited Little Havens, everything changed.
“You expect somewhere clinical and depressing, but it wasn’t like that at all. It was calm, peaceful… it just felt safe. Everyone spoke to us like human beings. It felt like they were living this with us, not just treating us.”
“In hospital everything feels urgent, but at Little Havens, time slowed down,” said Michael and Sarah. “And that’s when the Care Team started saying yes.”
The family carried Elio around the gardens, and the team arranged a photographer so they could have proper family photos, something the couple say they wouldn’t have thought to ask for.
“As the tubes and equipment were removed, it felt like we had our baby back,” they said. “We were able to do things that had felt impossible in hospital.”
They decorated Elio’s room with a piece of wallpaper from home and drawings from his big sister, and watched films together, lying on the bed as a family. Ob94b4.title: Airport and emergency services put to the test in major Stansted exercise
Ob94b4.text:
More than 400 people took part in a major emergency training exercise at London Stansted as emergency services and partner organisations rehearsed their response to a simulated aircraft accident.
The large-scale exercise took place on Tuesday 24 November and formed part of the airport's regular preparedness programme.
Teams from across the airport took part alongside colleagues from Essex Police, Essex County Fire and Rescue Service, East of England Ambulance Service, Essex & Herts Air Ambulance and a range of local and national partner organisations.
Using a decommissioned aircraft at the airport's Compass Base facility, the scenario tested how agencies would work together during a major incident.
Teams rehearsed every stage of the response, from rescuing casualties and treating injuries to managing communications and supporting passengers and their families.
The exercise was designed to challenge responders in a realistic environment and test plans, procedures and decision-making under pressure.
Nick Millar, Operations Director at London Stansted, said:
"Exercises of this scale don't happen overnight. Months of planning go into making them as realistic and challenging as possible, and we've been really pleased with how the day went. What stood out was the way everyone worked together. From our own airport teams to the emergency services and supporting agencies, there was a huge amount of professionalism, teamwork and commitment throughout the exercise.
"While an aircraft accident is an extremely unlikely event, it's important that we regularly put our plans to the test so we're prepared for any situation. These exercises give us the opportunity to learn from each other, identify any improvements we can make and strengthen the already strong relationships we have with our emergency service partners. I'd like to thank everyone who took part and helped make the exercise such a success."
Essex Police Chief Inspector Julia Finch, Stansted Airport Commander , said:
“This was a very successful exercise which really tested our skills and preparedness for a significant incident. It’s really important that we regularly test our capabilities to ensure we’re ready for any eventuality."
Station Manager Amir Williamson from Essex County Fire and Rescue Service's Emergency Planning Team said:
"An aircraft incident presents particular challenges for firefighters, so the chance to train in this setting alongside airport crews and our emergency service partners is valuable. The exercise tested our response at operational, tactical and strategic levels, helping us practice how we would bring our skills and resources together to rescue people and save lives."
Steve Brant, Resilience Manager, East of England Ambulance Service, said:
"The exercise at London Stansted Airport provided an important opportunity to test how agencies would work together during a complex emergency. Exercises like this help us strengthen our plans and ensure we remain prepared to provide the best possible care and support, while reassuring the public that emergency services are ready to respond when needed."
Essex & Herts Air Ambulance also played a key role in the exercise, with clinicians taking part in a highly realistic training scenario developed by members of its own team.
Ben Myer, who led the exercise for the Essex & Herts Air Ambulance, said:
"This was the culmination of months of planning and a massive commitment from the Essex & Herts Air Ambulance team. We faced a high-fidelity scenario involving manikins and live casualty actors with realistic injuries and responses to treatment. It was an opportunity to respond, test and learn, while working collaboratively with our partner services in an exercise environment."
The exercise will now be reviewed by participating organisations, with lessons identified and shared to help further strengthen emergency preparedness and multi-agency response arrangements.

O3d569.title: My Life in Business
O3d569.text:
Peter Richardson, Publishing Editor at BusinessTime in Essex, gets the ball rolling on a new feature on Business Wire in Essex – My Life in Business.
MY working life started back in 1978 (yes, I know, it’s quite a while back now!) when, at the age of 19, I joined the East Anglian Daily Times as a junior reporter.
James Callaghan was Prime Minister and the winter of discontent lie just ahead. More pertinently, I was writing my stories on a manual typewriter. Younger readers might want to Google winter of discontent and manual typewriter!
I’d long wanted to be a journalist, but what I really wanted was to be the next Brian Moore or John Motson football commentator. A stint on a regional newspaper was a mere short-term stepping stone, I thought. First lesson in adult life learned – keep your dreams realistic!
Instead of creating my own, ‘they think it’s all over’ moment’, I spent 12 very happy years in regional journalism, firstly reporting on some great stories (I spent a wet November afternoon trapsing around a north Essex graveyard looking for, and finding, the grave of Jack the Ripper – I’ll give the details to anyone who’s interested!) before climbing the greasy pole of promotion. The top of the pole culminated in me being appointed Group Editor of a 22-edion group of newspapers covering Essex and Greater London.
It was a largely hugely enjoyable time, but the pay was not great. I was paid for working a 37-hour week, but my average working week soaked up twice those hours. With a mortgage and two young children, I decided if I was working 70+ hours a week, I might as well try getting paid for most of those hours. I had started doing a little freelance media relations/PR work on the side (well, the kids had to be fed!) and soon realised there was much more money to be earned in PR than there was being a Newspaper Group Editor.
So, at 3am one morning I sat bolt upright in bed and proclaimed to my startled wife I was going to quit my job and work for myself. The most important decision of my working life had been made.
Whenever I look back, it still scares me at the magnitude of the decision. As I said, I had a mortgage and two young children – yet something just told me at that moment, it was the right decision. Second lesson in adult life learned – follow your gut instinct.

Ocfc11.text:
Older people experiencing a mental health crisis are being supported to manage their wellbeing at home, thanks to therapeutic resources funded by Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust’s (EPUT) charity.
Charitable funding has enabled EPUT’s Functional Intensive Response and Support Team (FIRST) in south Essex to buy a range of practical resources to help patients through a crisis and, wherever possible, avoid the need for a hospital admission.
The team provides intensive support to older adults, visiting patients in their own homes and working alongside their families and other clinical teams to help them manage their mental health and build confidence.
The items funded include whiteboards and pens, notebooks, large-print puzzles, creative materials, portable CD players and CDs, sensory items and fidget toys.
Occupational Therapist Laura Dawson uses the resources to help patients manage anxiety, improve concentration and motivation, and engage in meaningful activities.
Laura said: “These resources have been really beneficial for our patients. Practical activities help people develop a greater sense of calm, regain confidence in their abilities and rediscover enjoyment in activities. Having these resources means we can try different approaches and find what works for each person.
“Each item has a different purpose. Whiteboards can act as memory prompts, help patients set weekly goals or plan a daily routine, while notebooks provide a space to write down thoughts and feelings.
“Creative activities can improve concentration and motivation while giving people a sense of achievement. Silk painting has proved particularly effective because it is accessible and allows people to create something they can feel proud of relatively quickly.
“Music can support relaxation, mindfulness and anxiety management, while stress putty, fidget toys and other sensory items can help people manage agitation and self-soothe.
Laura added: “One of the benefits is that people can try something before they or their family buy it themselves. If listening to music, doing a creative activity or using a sensory item helps, they’ve found another way to support their wellbeing.
“It’s about giving people practical strategies they can use when we’re not there, alongside support from the wider clinical team. We want to help people through the immediate crisis and give them tools that can support their ongoing recovery.”
The resources are shared between occupational therapists working across FIRST teams in Southend, Basildon and Chelmsford, extending the benefits to more patients and carers.
EPUT Charitable Funds help provide activities and improvements beyond what the NHS would normally fund, enhancing patients’ experiences and supporting their health and wellbeing.

O33c43.title: UN Special Rapporteur helps shape new housing laws
O33c43.text:
United Nations Special Rapporteur Dr Koldo Casla has helped shape new housing laws in Spain following a high-profile homeless case which sparked nationwide protests and triggered a national election.
Dr Koldo Casla , a Senior Lecturer at Essex Law School and the Human Rights Centre, engaged constructively with government ministers in the wake of 87-year-old, Maricarmen Abascal’s eviction from her home.
A decree-law that aims to give better protections to vulnerable tenants has since been passed, with the Minister for Housing, Isabel Rodriguez, highlighting Dr Casla’s contribution to the new law in Parliament.
Dr Casla’s intervention came in his capacity as the UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Adequate Housing.
Dr Casla was appointed Special Rapporteur by the UN Human Rights Council in March 2026.
He has the responsibility of assisting the United Nations and Member States in implementing laws and policies to satisfy the right to housing.
As well as numerous high-profile media appearances in Spain, Dr Casla engaged with the authorities to push for legal changes to ensure there is no repeat of the Maricarmen case.
His representations included the urgent need for new legislation to protect the vulnerable from eviction, the introduction of mandatory proportionality tests in all evictions, and tighter anti-speculation measures in Spain’s housing market.
Dr Casla said: “Maricarmen’s case was a painful reminder that Spain’s law had significant shortcomings in relation to the right to housing.
"I am determined to continue collaborating with whatever future government after the election of 29 November to fulfil the promise of article 47 of the Spanish Constitution, which proclaims the right to housing.”
Alongside his work in Spain, Dr Casla made an official 12-day visit to Ghana in October as Special Rapporteur, where he urged the government to introduce stronger protections for tenants, put an end to forced evictions, set realistic targets for affordable housing, and encourage the use of locally sourced materials in construction.
Dr Casla is also preparing his first thematic report for the UN Human Rights Council on a topic that resonates with Human Rights Local, a project of Essex’s Human Rights Centre, which he launched in 2020.
The report will explore best practices from local governments and community-led initiatives around the world to make the human rights to housing real and effective at the local level.
Dr Casla’s work at the United Nations is informed by his research on the social function of housing, including his most recent book The Social Right to Property.

O112fb.title: Marine scientist unlocks secrets of the deep for BBC’s Blue Planet III
O112fb.text:
A marine biologist whose pioneering research has uncovered some of the ocean’s most elusive creatures has helped shine a light on the mysteries of the deep for the BBC’s Blue Planet III.
Dr Michelle Taylor , from the School of Life Sciences , advised producers behind the Sir David Attenborough-fronted smash hit.
Dr Taylor helped shape Sunday’s episode, which ventures into the depths of the oceans to explore what has been described as “the last great frontier on earth”.
The Senior Lecturer, who is also Head of Science at Ocean Census , reviewed the science and connected the production team with other experts.
Her expertise was sought following pioneering research that has led to the discovery of coral reefs in Antarctica and helped capture the only confirmed footage of a colossal squid in the wild .
She has also had a species of coral , seaspider, and sea cucumber named in her honour.
Dr Taylor said: “It’s always a pleasure to work with the BBC Natural History unit and I’m thrilled that Blue Planet III is being aired – the cinematography and story-telling when applied to the deep-sea animals brings that relatively unknown realm to life.
“The deep-sea is the largest habitat on Earth and has a plethora of ecosystems that this episode highlights. I’m thrilled that so many exciting animal stories of the deep will be shown to the world.”
Explore the gallery below to relive some of Dr Taylor's exciting expeditions
Dr Michelle Taylor and Oenone Scott on board
The episode, which airs on November 29, and is live on iPlayer , explored the Pacific and Arctic ocean basins. It showcases a range of creatures, including the ‘flying spaghetti monster’, a young female argonaut, and forests of hidden coral.
This is the second time Dr Taylor has worked with producers, helping the team behind Blue Planet II in 2017 as well.
Away from the series national treasure Sir David is no stranger to Essex, having been awarded an honorary degree in 1987 .
Professor Terry McGenity , Head of the School of Life Sciences, said: “The deep ocean has a remarkable array of different habitats.
“Its inhabitants are vital for life on Earth, from abundant microbes, recycling nutrients, controlling climate, providing medicines and underpinning food webs, to the amazing and enigmatic animals that Dr Taylor and her team are discovering.
“It is hoped that Blue Planet III will inspire the current and next generation of leaders to create joined-up policy that better recognises the connectedness of all habitats on Earth, and that considers both biodiversity and climate.
“In the School of Life Sciences, we share our excellent research with students, the wider world and policy makers. "Dr Michelle Taylor’s expert contributions help to shed light on the (mostly) dark, deep ocean in an entertaining and thought-provoking way.”

O5114a.title: First 276 Homes Approved in the Gilston Area
O5114a.text:
The first 276 homes in Village 7 of the Gilston Area have been approved by East Herts Council, marking a significant milestone for Harlow and Gilston Garden Town.
With plans for future residents to generate and share clean energy, grow their own food and enjoy restored historic buildings, the first 276 homes will include 39 for affordable rent and 26 for shared ownership.
The Village 7 layout, which will include 1500 homes in total, is designed to make walking, cycling and public transport practical alternatives to driving.
Measures include separate walking and cycling routes through Church Lane Green, connections to the planned public transport corridor and more than 1000 cycle parking spaces.
Secure cycle storage within homes and apartment buildings, alongside visitor parking near play areas and green spaces, will help make cycling convenient for everyday journeys.
Raised community growing beds will give residents opportunities to grow food together, including spaces near apartments where private outdoor space is more limited.
A foraging trail featuring fruiting plants will run through the neighbourhood, alongside a sensory garden offering a quieter place to sit and enjoy the surroundings.
A play area inspired by the area’s farming heritage will include references to rare British farm breeds. Five smaller ‘play-on-the-way’ spaces will provide opportunities for children to play along everyday walking and cycling routes.
Every home will also connect to a shared heating and hot-water network. The Community Heat Hub, approved as part of an earlier infrastructure application, will be operational before the first residents move in.
Village 7 is being delivered by Taylor Wimpey. Its masterplan, approved in April, also includes a new football hub and the restoration of listed barns for office and community use.
Councillor Maura Connolly, Executive Member for Planning and Growth at East Herts Council, said: “This is a major moment for Gilston.
“After years of planning, we have approved the first 276 homes, including 65 affordable homes, in a development that will shape this area for generations.
“But what makes Village 7 particularly exciting is how it brings people together, whether that’s growing food, sharing clean energy, playing sport or making use of historic buildings given a new purpose.
“These features matter. They help create a community, alongside the homes people need, and we want them to be central to how Gilston develops.”
Jonathan Locke, Head of Planning at Taylor Wimpey North Thames, said: “This approval is a big step forward for Village 7 and the Gilston area.
“We can now start work on what will become the gateway to a highly sustainable new community, with the first 276 homes being built at the same time as significantareas of new public green space that will allow people to relax, play and look after the planet.
“We have carefully designed our homes to be fit for the future. They combine attractive architecture and modern layouts with a range of eco-friendly features and construction measures to make them car bonnet-zero ready.
“We are going much further than the requirements in our outline planning permission on carbon reduction and sustainability, both to create the best possible homes for future residents and to make a positive contribution towards the climate emergency.”
Harlow and Gilston Garden Town brings together plans for new homes, jobs, transport links and community facilities in and around Harlow, across the Hertfordshire and Essex border.
The Gilston area will comprise seven new villages, with plans for 10,000 homes alongside schools, green spaces and other infrastructure.

O852d7.title: Press Release: Brightlingsea Councillors oppose proposals for 550 homes to be included in Local Plan
O852d7.text:
Ward Councillors representing Brightlingsea have voiced their opposition to Trinity College’s request that their land on the outskirts of the town should be included in the updated Local Plan.
Local Councillors were successful in having the original application by Trinity for 300 homes deleted from the draft plan earlier this year, but the College has resubmitted detailed plans to use a wider area of land on both sides of Church Road to build 550 homes.
(Proposed areas marked in red belong to Trinity College)
Councillor Jayne Chapman spoke out on the issue at the meeting of the Planning Policy and Local Plan Committee on 17th November 2026, and Councillor Mick Barry highlighted his opposition to the plans at the full Tendring District Council (TDC) meeting on Tuesday 24th November 2026.
They have pledged to co-ordinate a response from the Town Council and community representatives to support Tendring District Council Planning Officers in opposing the proposals.
Ward Councillors will request further information on the proposals and hold meetings with interested parties in the town to gather local knowledge. This will support Officers in preparing submissions to the Independent Inspector for the hearings when they are scheduled in 2027.

Od755a.source: Bernard Jenkin MP (Harwich and North Essex) in Parliament
Od755a.text:
I join others in thanking you for the privilege of serving under your chairmanship, Sir Jeremy. I declare two interests: first, that I am a vice-president of Combat Stress—I will come on to how I got that role in a moment—and secondly, that I married the sister of Johnny Strutt, the constituent of my right hon. Friend the Member for Witham (Priti Patel) . She is in the Gallery supporting her colleagues and her brother. It is an honour to stand here to represent the interests of the Welsh Guards.
To pick up on the point made by the right hon. Member for Dwyfor Meirionnydd (Liz Saville Roberts) , what national or public interest is served by retaining these documents in secret? That is what the Minister has to answer. I notice she has been listening intently to everything that is being said, and I hope she will take the opportunity, if she has not done so already, to greet the former Welsh Guards in the Public Gallery and listen to their testimony. [Interruption.] She has already done so—let us put that on the record—or she will.
I want to add a quite different emphasis. This is not about finding blame; things do go wrong in war and tragedies happen. Incidentally, the Welsh Guards should be honoured for their contribution to winning the campaign, just as much as any other battalion or military formation. They played their part. We lost ships and we lost men, who died in battle because war means taking losses. What happened to them does not detract from them, and the blame heaped on them tells us there is something to be uncovered. Some people are hiding things for their own interests, not for the national or public interest.
I knew Johnny for many years before I understood what he had been through, and I met my good friend Crispin Black many times before I understood what he had been through. It was only because I was shadow Defence Secretary and met Surgeon Commander Rick Jolly, who was there in the field hospital at Ajax bay and treated so many of the casualties on the day, that I understood the reality of what happened and the trauma it left. That is why I am a vice-president of Combat Stress. The unresolved nature of the trauma makes it so much worse. They are unable to explain to themselves, the public, their friends or their military comrades why what happened happened.
A new book, the next edition of “Too Thin for a Shroud”, is coming out. If anyone has not read the book that is already out, it does not take long to read. It is absolutely shocking. Many things happened that should not have, and the bombing of Sir Galahad was just one of them. The new book will reveal so much more because a lot of the witnesses to the inquiry have released their testimony voluntarily. Good on them.
But what about the people who refused to do so? I attach no blame to them because reputations are at stake. It is in the public interest for this information to come out, because it is evident— the hon. Member for Llanelli (Dame Nia Griffith) touched on this—that a system failure was at fault. The command chain was wrongly established. There was no single in-theatre commander able to make decisions. The maritime taskforce commander, Sandy Woodward, said in his biography, “I knew this was wrong. I knew I should have stopped it. I so regret I didn’t stop it”, or words to that effect. But it was not under his command; it was not under land command. The amphibious taskforce and the land and maritime components were all separately commanded from Northwood—very long screwdrivers and communication chains. Nobody in theatre was individually or jointly responsible for the whole operation.
Others have testified to me casually and in writing, including Admiral Chris Parry, whose last job was at the Development, Concepts and Doctrine Centre at Shrivenham. Oc4bc9.title: Victorian Christmas Market raises £6k for charity
Oc4bc9.text:
Festive season begins with charity Christmas Market
MUSIC, performances, stalls and food ushered in the festive season with Tendring’s biggest charity Christmas market on Saturday.
Community Voluntary Services Together (CVST) hosted its annual Victorian Christmas Market at Clacton Town Hall on Saturday, 14th November.
Shoppers were welcomed in by festive music from the Salvation Army band and volunteers dressed in Victorian outfits on the door.
Inside there were 26 charity stalls selling Christmas decorations, fairtrade items, toys, jewellery, gifts and more – with all money raised on each stall kept by that charity.
More than £6,000 was raised on the day for charities and good causes.
Lisa Andrews, chief executive of CVST, said: “The Victorian Christmas market is our flagship event and not only does it support us as a charity, but it’s our way of supporting charities and good causes in Tendring at Christmas time too.
“It was such a lovely atmosphere and really got us all into the Christmas spirit.
“We had a scrooge, some amazing Victorian dresses, and truly beautiful stalls.
“Plus, the wonderful performances including those from Young Minds Dementia Choir, Kaleidoscope, SingalongaPen, Seated Dance, Princes Youth Theatre, the Panto stars, and more.
“Thank you to everyone for making such an effort with the decorations and costumes and really making the event so brilliant.”
Competition…
The winner of best costume was Kevin Burns from the Clacton branch of Parkinsons UK, while the winner of the best decorated stall was Grassroots charity – winners each won a free stall for next years’ event.
